Pool Filter Cleaning in Phoenix

Every pool in the Valley has a filter doing quiet, constant work against dust, pollen, sunscreen and hard-water minerals. When it clogs, the water clouds and the pump strains. One free call, any hour, puts you through to an independent, locally owned pool service company.

  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Pool Filter Cleaning

Pool filter cleaning in Phoenix is one of those jobs nobody notices until it is overdue. A filter that is packed with dust from the last storm, oils from swimmers and fine mineral grit from hard water forces the pump to work harder and lets cloudy water win. This page compares the three filter types, explains what a professional clean involves for each one, covers where dirty filter water may and may not go, and helps you read the pressure gauge at a safe, homeowner level.

A quick word on who is talking. Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro does not clean filters or sell parts. It is a free phone line: call (623) 240-0428 any hour, an automated assistant takes a short description of the filter problem, and the call is passed to an independent, locally owned pool service company that cleans, quotes and bills you directly.

Cartridge, DE or sand: how each filter traps dirt

Every pool filter does the same job: water from the pump passes through a material that holds back dirt and lets clean water return to the pool. What differs is the material, how fine a particle it can catch, and how it gets cleaned. Pool & Spa News, a trade publication for pool technicians, covers the care of each type; the table below sums up the general differences.

Cartridge, DE and sand pool filters compared: how they trap dirt, how they are cleaned and common replacement parts
Filter typeHow it traps dirtHow fine it filtersHow it is cleanedParts that wear out
CartridgeWater passes through pleated fabric wrapped around a core. The pleats give a large surface area in a small tank.Finer than sand, not as fine as DENo backwash. The tank is opened, the cartridges come out and are rinsed, and sometimes soaked in a cleaner made for filters.Cartridge elements, tank O-ring, air relief valve, pressure gauge
DE (diatomaceous earth)A powder made from fossilized diatoms coats fabric grids inside the tank and forms a filter cake that does the actual filtering.The finest of the threeBackwashed between cleanings, then taken apart so the grids can be hosed off. Fresh DE powder is added every time.Grids, manifold, standpipe O-ring, backwash valve parts
SandWater filters down through a deep bed of filter sand in the tank.The coarsest of the threeBackwashed: flow is reversed to lift the dirt out to waste. The sand itself is replaced every several years.Filter sand, laterals at the bottom of the tank, multiport valve spider gasket

Sand and DE filters send pool water out to waste each time they are backwashed, and that water has to be replaced, which matters in a desert where every gallon is refilled from the tap. Cartridge filters avoid backwashing, which is one reason many Valley pools use them. The tradeoff is that cartridges have to be taken out and rinsed by hand.

Which pool filter is best for a Phoenix pool?

There is no single answer. A careful pool technician looks at three things before suggesting a change. First, the pump's flow rate: Pool & Spa News notes that filters that need cleaning again and again after short runs often have too much water pushed through them, meaning the filter may be undersized or the pump too powerful. Second, how the pool is used, since heavy swimming and lots of sunscreen load a filter faster. Third, how much handling you can live with. A DE filter gives the clearest water but needs fresh powder after every backwash and careful disposal of the spent powder. If someone recommends a new filter, ask why the current one cannot be repaired and ask to see the pump and filter ratings side by side. The pool equipment repair page covers the rest of the pad.

What a professional pool filter cleaning service involves

The steps differ by filter. Each starts the same way: pump off, pressure released, and a look at the gauge before and after so you can see the difference.

Cartridge filter clean

The technician turns the pump off at the timer or automation, opens the air relief valve to bleed pressure, then removes the tank lid and lifts out the cartridges. Each element is hosed pleat by pleat and checked for tears, flattened pleats, cracked end caps and a soft or crushed core. If oils or mineral scale are baked into the fabric, a soak in a cleaner made for filters may follow. The tank O-ring is inspected and lubricated, the lid is reseated, air is bled, and the clean starting pressure is written down.

DE filter clean

A DE filter is usually backwashed first, then opened so the grid assembly can come out. Each grid is hosed and checked, especially along the seams where the fabric meets the frame, because even a small opening lets powder through. The manifold and standpipe O-ring are checked for cracks. After the filter is closed and running, the technician adds the correct amount of fresh DE for that filter's size through the skimmer, since too much powder can bridge between the grids.

Sand filter service

Routine sand care is a backwash and a rinse setting on the multiport valve. A fuller service checks whether the bed has packed into channels, which lets water slip past the sand, and whether sand is showing up on the pool floor, a sign of a broken lateral. If backwashing no longer brings the pressure down, the technician can tell you whether the sand or the laterals are the problem.

On any filter, a careful technician also looks at the things that make a filter clog early: low chlorine, algae starting in corners, or a pump basket that is cracked and letting leaves through.

Backwash and rinse water: where it may go in Phoenix

Dirty filter water is not just water. It carries dust, organic debris, chlorine and, for DE filters, spent powder. Cities in the Valley treat it as something to keep out of the street and the storm drain, because storm drains run untreated to washes and rivers. Rules differ from city to city, so check your own city's page before anyone backwashes.

For the City of Phoenix, the Water Services Department tells residents to reuse backwash water on landscaping on their own property or to send larger amounts down the home's sanitary sewer cleanout, and not to drain into the street, an alley or other city right-of-way. Under City Code Chapter 32C, pool water may not go to the storm drain. Phoenix allows clean, dechlorinated water to reach the right-of-way only by permit and only for homes with no sewer cleanout, and it lists pool backwash as prohibited from that route.

Mesa spells out DE handling in more detail. Its drain and backwash page recommends a separation tank for DE and cellulose fiber filters to capture the powder, and says spent DE can be dried, bagged and put in the trash. Mesa also says cartridge rinse water should go over gravel, lawn or another planted area. If you live in Scottsdale, Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale or another city, look up that city's own rules; the guide to draining a pool in Arizona collects more of them.

DE powder is a dust to respect. Some diatomaceous earth sold for pool filters contains crystalline silica, and NIOSH links breathing respirable crystalline silica to serious lung disease. Do not pour or sweep dry DE where people breathe it, keep the bag away from children and pets, and read the product's safety data sheet. Many homeowners leave DE handling to their pool company for this reason.

Pool filter pressure: low, high and what to check

The round gauge on top of the filter tank is the best tool you have. After a filter is freshly cleaned and the pump is at its normal speed, note the reading. That is your clean starting pressure. Angi's filter cleaning guide and Pool & Spa News both use a rise of about 8 to 10 psi above normal as the usual point to clean or backwash, and your filter's own manual may give a different figure. The filter cleaning schedule guide explains how to use that rise to plan cleanings by season.

Pool filter pressure symptoms, likely causes and safe homeowner checks
What you seeWhat it often points toSafe check you can doWhen to call
Pressure 8 to 10 psi over the clean readingA dirty filterNote the reading and the dateIf you are not comfortable opening the filter, or a cleaning is due
Pressure lower than normal, weak returnsNot enough water reaching the pump: full baskets, low water, a suction air leakEmpty the skimmer and pump baskets; check the water is about halfway up the skimmer openingIf baskets are clean, the level is right and pressure stays low
Air bubbles in the pump lid or from the returnsLow water, a leaking lid O-ring, a split cleaner hose or a suction leakCheck the water level and look for an obvious hose splitIf bubbles continue; a leak on the suction side needs a technician
Pressure stays high right after cleaningMedia caked with oils or scale, a closed valve, or a pump larger than the filterConfirm valves are in their usual positionsCall: the media or the plumbing needs a closer look
DE or sand on the pool floorA torn grid, a cracked manifold, a broken lateral or too much DENone beyond noting what you seeCall: the filter needs to be opened and inspected

Safety at the filter. A filter tank holds water under pressure. Never loosen a filter clamp or lid while the pump is running. Turn the pump off and open the air relief valve first, and if you are unsure, leave it closed and call. Do not open motor covers or electrical boxes. If a breaker or GFCI has tripped, you can reset it once; if it trips again, stop and call a pool technician.

Signs a cartridge or DE grid needs replacing

Cleaning brings a filter back only so far. HomeGuide's filter cost guide says cartridges usually need replacing every two to three years, and a cartridge that is torn, cracked or loose at the end caps should be replaced sooner. These are the signs a pool technician looks for.

  • Torn, frayed or flattened pleats on a cartridge, or end caps that are cracked or pulling away.
  • A clean starting pressure that keeps creeping up after each cleaning, even when the cartridge looks clean.
  • DE coming back into the pool, which can point to torn grid fabric or a cracked manifold.
  • Sand on the pool floor or very short runs between backwashes on a sand filter.
  • Water that stays hazy with good chlorine and normal run times.

Why filters work harder in the Valley

Phoenix pools face a mix that many pools elsewhere do not. City of Phoenix tap water is hard, as its annual water quality report shows. Calcium and magnesium in that water can leave scale on surfaces and in filter fabric as water evaporates in the heat and is topped off again. Summer storms add a different load. The National Weather Service's official monsoon season runs June 15 to September 30, and its Phoenix office describes the thunderstorm-driven dust walls called haboobs, which can drop a fine layer of dirt into every open pool in a neighborhood. The monsoon pool care guide covers what to do before and after those storms.

A pool that is not filtered for long enough turns green, and a green pool is a safety problem as much as a cleaning one: the bottom cannot be seen, and children should be kept well away from it. Standing green water can also breed mosquitoes; Maricopa County Environmental Services takes mosquito and green pool complaints at 602-506-6616. If it has already turned, the green pool cleanup page explains the recovery.

Pool filter cleaning cost

Published numbers are a rough guide only. HomeGuide's 2026 pool cost guides estimate about $110 for a professional visit to inspect, diagnose and clean a filter, give replacement cartridges a broad range of roughly $30 to $200 each, and put professional sand replacement at about $100 to $250. Angi estimates $20 to $40 in supplies if a homeowner cleans a cartridge filter. None of these is this line's price. Whichever local pool company takes your call names its own figure after seeing your filter, and real quotes in the Valley vary with filter size, condition and whether parts are needed. The pool service cost guide covers weekly plans, which often include filter cleaning on a set schedule.

Questions to ask the pool company

  • Is filter cleaning included in a weekly plan, and how often, or is it a separate visit?
  • What was the pressure before and after, and what should my clean starting pressure be?
  • Did you see torn pleats, grid damage or broken laterals? Can I see them?
  • Where will the backwash or rinse water go, and how will spent DE be handled?
  • If you recommend a new cartridge, grid set or filter, what is the written price for each option?

Cleaning a filter is generally treated as routine service. Replacing a filter, valves or plumbing is repair work, and for that the license check below applies.

Check the license first. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) licenses contractors, and its residential classifications include R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair. Repairs, equipment replacement and resurfacing generally call for a licensed contractor; whether a cleaning-only service needs a license is not spelled out, so ask the ROC if it matters to you. Ask the company for its ROC license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search (opens in a new tab) before work begins. The line does not check this for you.

Filter pressure high, low or bouncing? Call any hour, say whether it is a cartridge, DE or sand filter and what the gauge reads, and you will be put through to a local pool company.

Common questions

How much does pool filter cleaning cost?

HomeGuide's 2026 pool cost guides put a professional visit to inspect, diagnose and clean a filter at about $110, and list replacement cartridges at roughly $30 to $200 each. Those are published national estimates, not prices from this line. The pool company you are put through to sets its own price after it sees the filter, and real Phoenix quotes vary with the filter type, its size and its condition.

Which pool filter do I need?

All three common types can keep a home pool clear. Cartridge filters skip backwashing and use the least water. DE filters catch the finest particles but need the most handling. Sand filters are the simplest to run and catch the coarsest dirt. The right size depends on your pump's flow rate, so ask a pool company to check that the filter and pump are matched before you replace either one.

Why is my pool filter pressure low?

Low pressure usually means the pump is not getting enough water. Check the skimmer and pump baskets for leaves and debris, and check that the water sits about halfway up the skimmer opening. If the baskets are clean and the level is right, air may be leaking into the suction side or the impeller may be clogged, and those are jobs for a pool technician.

Why is my pool filter not working even though the pump runs?

A filter can look like it is running while doing little. The media may be torn, channeled or caked solid, the internal parts may be cracked, or the pump may be pushing more water than the filter is rated for. Signs include cloudy water with normal pressure, DE or sand blowing back into the pool, or pressure that will not drop after cleaning. A pool technician can open the filter and inspect it.

Who cleans pool filters in the Phoenix area?

Pool service companies do, either as part of a weekly route or as a one-time visit. Call the free line any hour, say what kind of filter you have and what the pressure gauge reads, and you will be put through to an independent local pool company that quotes and does the work itself.
